title: Revising a diagnosis of functional neurological disorder—a case report
case_prompt:
A 62-year-old woman was referred to neuropsychiatry with a 3-year history of gradually progressive dysphonia, difficulty keeping her eyes open, and falls. Her medical history included COPD, type 2 diabetes, ischaemic heart disease, hypertension, stage 3b chronic kidney disease, and anaemia. One year after symptom onset, otorhinolaryngology evaluation showed slowed hypopharyngeal and laryngeal movements on laryngoscopy, with normal orofacial muscle function but effortful and delayed vocal production; communication was often supplemented with hand gestures. Neurological examination at that time was reportedly normal apart from variable vocal output, and a brain MRI was unremarkable. A diagnosis of functional voice disorder was made, and she underwent inpatient rehabilitation for FND.

Three years after symptom onset, she reported increasing falls and withdrawal from cooking and outdoor activities, without mood symptoms. The Montreal Cognitive Assessment score was 22/30. Neurological examination demonstrated aphonia, eyelid apraxia, blepharospasm, near-constant use of sunglasses indoors, and frequent touching of the corner of her eyes (a sensory geste). A repeat MRI with susceptibility-weighted imaging showed hypointense signal in the substantia nigra, red nuclei, and globus pallidus, suggestive of iron deposition. A CT scan of the head showed no intracerebral calcification. The diagnosis was then revised to an atypical akinetic rigid syndrome.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Functional voice disorder was questioned when laryngoscopy demonstrated objective hypokinetic movements of the larynx, which are “unlikely to be explained by FND…”  
2. Inherited neurodegeneration with brain-iron accumulation syndromes were considered given the SWI findings of iron deposition, as “neurodegeneration with brain-iron accumulation … were considered as potential differential diagnoses…”  
3. Negative genetic testing for known NBIA genes excluded these disorders, as “No pathogenic mutations identified within the following: ATP7B, c19orf12, CP, FTL, PANK2, PLA2G6, SLC30A10, SLC39A14, WDR45.”  
4. Aceruloplasminemia was specifically highlighted because of her age, raised ferritin, red nucleus involvement, and diabetes mellitus: “with special emphasis on aceruloplasminemia in light of the age-at-onset, raised serum ferritin, radiological evidence of red nucleus involvement and the presence of type-2 diabetes mellitus.”  
5. Aceruloplasminemia was ruled out by normal ceruloplasmin and genetic testing, as “normal serum ceruloplasmin concentration and negative ceruloplasmin gene (CP) genetic testing ruled out aceruloplasminemia.”  
6. Progressive supranuclear palsy was supported by clinical features of Parkinsonism, ocular movement impairment, dysarthria, and falls, and by characteristic iron deposition on SWI, consistent with “PSP is a 4-repeat tauopathy, characterized clinically by gait-disturbance, Parkinsonian features, impaired ocular movement, neuropsychiatric changes, dysarthria and falls” and “Basal ganglia iron deposition has been described in PSP...”
